item.content:encoded: Awar Odhiang featured in Vogue wearing a floral printed dress and sculpted oversized rose headpiece. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Remember the model who turned the finale of Matthieu Blazy ‘s first Chanel show into one of the most talked-about runway moments of 2025? That was Awar Odhiang, and she has another major reason to celebrate. The South Sudanese-Canadian model has been named Model of the Year at The Fashion Awards 2026. The 25-year-old will receive the honour at London’s Royal Albert Hall on 30 November. Born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia and raised in Canada, Awar’s journey to the international fashion scene has taken her from being discovered in Alberta to walking some of the world’s biggest runways. She is now represented by major modelling agencies across London, Milan, Paris and New York. Awar Odhiang walking the red carpet at the 2026 Met Gala in New York City. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Her runway résumé includes shows for Prada, Versace, Miu Miu, Saint Laurent and Jacquemus, but it was her appearance at Chanel’s Spring/Summer 2026 show in October 2025 that introduced her to an even wider audience. Closing Matthieu Blazy’s first collection for the fashion house, Awar wore the show’s bridal look, featuring an oversized white shirt and a voluminous, colourful feathered skirt. But it was what happened at the finale that captured everyone’s attention. As the models gathered for their final walk, Awar broke formation, smiling, clapping and twirling in her skirt. When Blazy appeared, she ran towards him and embraced him. The spontaneous moment quickly went viral, with fashion fans celebrating the joy she brought to the runway. It was also a historic appearance: Awar became only the third Black woman to close a Chanel show in the house’s 115-year history, after Alek Wek and Adut Akech. Model of the Year 2026 winner Awar Odhiang backstage at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Since then, her career has continued to gather pace. Awar has appeared on eight international magazine covers this year and fronted campaigns for Chanel, Chloé, Louis Vuitton, Saint Laurent, Loro Piana and H&M. She has also used her growing platform to speak up for greater representation and inclusion of Black models in the luxury fashion industry. Awar Odhiang in Daniel Roseberry’s Schiaparelli Spring 2026 Haute Couture collection in Paris. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Her Model of the Year recognition celebrates a remarkable year of runway, editorial and campaign work, as well as the influence she continues to have beyond the catwalk. On 30 November, she’ll take that recognition to the Royal Albert Hall, adding another milestone to a career that is still unfolding. Awar Odhiang wearing a tailored blazer during international fashion week. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Awar Odhiang attending the 2026 Met Gala in custom Chanel by Matthieu Blazy. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram The post Awar Odhiang Named Model of the Year at The Fashion Awards 2026 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: NASA's secret weapon in the lunar space race may be ... procurement reform?
item.description: Senior NASA officials held a lengthy news conference last weekend, laying out a series of lunar contract awards, new contract opportunities, and mission decisions. They followed one after the other: landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power generation, storage, and communication satellites. It never seemed to end. "Hopefully, we're keeping industry on their toes trying to catch up to all the solicitations we're doing," said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, more than 90 minutes into the news conference. "This is what it takes to do the Moon Base in the timeline we have set forth." Read full article Comments

item.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
item.description: It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’ A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino. If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”. Continue reading...

item.title: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
item.description: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a pla
item.dc:creator: Alix Freckelton
item.content:encoded: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences. For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet. Is the air breathable? NASA illustration of Kepler-186f, the first Earth-size planet to be discovered in a habitable zone. (Image credit: NASA Ames/SETI Institute/JPL-CalTech via Wikimedia Commons) Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air? In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe. Atmospheric pressure matters just as much . At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs. Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal. Searching for life An artist illustration of exoplanet K2-18b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. (Image credit: Hubble, M. Kornmesser via Wikimedia commons) But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there? Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth . This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far. Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b , an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed . Astronomers can study the starlight that filters through exoplanet atmospheres, searching for signatures of molecules that may be signs of life. (Image credit: NASA, ESA and A. Feild (STScI)) The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation. Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star. More than Earth Mark 2 (Image credit: Audible) Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge. The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster. We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets. "Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately. One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary , The Martian ), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo. Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately. View Deal

item.title: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces its 3rd Edition in Republic of Benin | November 12th – 13th
item.description: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces the third edition of the event, taking place on November 12–13, 2026, in Cotonou, Republic of Benin. Following its previous edition, which brought together more than 6,700 participants and over 3,000 industry professionals, this pan-African gathering dedicated to the cultural and creative industries returns with a clear ambition: African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence. SIMA 2026 is supported by major institutional and private-sector partners, including the Ministry of Culture, Arts and Heritage of Benin,the Ministry of Tourism and Foreign Trade of Benin,the Embassy of France in Côte d’Ivoire,the BOAD Foundation, as well as SACEM, Sony Music and Warner Music Africa. These partnerships reflect the growing interest in the development and structuring of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. For the second consecutive year, Benin will host SIMA, in line with the country’s broader efforts to strengthen the role of the cultural and creative industries in the structural transformation of its economy and to enhance its cultural influence at both regional and international levels. Co-founded in 2022 by cultural entrepreneur Mamby Diomandé and artist and producer Pit Baccardi , SIMA has established itself as a platform dedicated to structuring, connecting and developing Africa’s creative ecosystems. By placing music at the heart of a broader reflection on the transformation of culture and the creative industries, SIMA also seeks to address the technological shifts reshaping the sector—from artificial intelligence to new ways of creating, distributing and consuming content. At a time when Africa’s creative economy could generate up to 20 million jobs by 2030, the 2026 edition aims to take a further step forward by contributing to the positioning of African creativity as a powerful driver of soft power, value creation and international influence. “African music is no longer simply a cultural phenomenon: it has become a force of influence. Our challenge now is to transform this influence into sustainable economic power. SIMA aims to build connections between creators, investors, institutions and markets so that the international visibility of our talents translates into measurable data, content monetization, economic opportunities, jobs and value creation for the continent.” Mamby Diomandé , Co-Founder of SIMA Three Priorities for Turning Creativity into Economic Power To address the challenges of a rapidly evolving global market, SIMA 2026 will structure its programme around three key priorities. The first focuses on competitiveness and internationalization, with the aim of strengthening the economic performance of industry stakeholders and facilitating the international export of African talent. item.content:encoded: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces the third edition of the event, taking place on November 12–13, 2026, in Cotonou, Republic of Benin. Following its previous edition, which brought together more than 6,700 participants and over 3,000 industry professionals, this pan-African gathering dedicated to the cultural and creative industries returns with a clear ambition: African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence. SIMA 2026 is supported by major institutional and private-sector partners, including the Ministry of Culture, Arts and Heritage of Benin,the Ministry of Tourism and Foreign Trade of Benin,the Embassy of France in Côte d’Ivoire,the BOAD Foundation, as well as SACEM, Sony Music and Warner Music Africa. These partnerships reflect the growing interest in the development and structuring of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. For the second consecutive year, Benin will host SIMA, in line with the country’s broader efforts to strengthen the role of the cultural and creative industries in the structural transformation of its economy and to enhance its cultural influence at both regional and international levels. Co-founded in 2022 by cultural entrepreneur Mamby Diomandé and artist and producer Pit Baccardi , SIMA has established itself as a platform dedicated to structuring, connecting and developing Africa’s creative ecosystems. By placing music at the heart of a broader reflection on the transformation of culture and the creative industries, SIMA also seeks to address the technological shifts reshaping the sector—from artificial intelligence to new ways of creating, distributing and consuming content. At a time when Africa’s creative economy could generate up to 20 million jobs by 2030, the 2026 edition aims to take a further step forward by contributing to the positioning of African creativity as a powerful driver of soft power, value creation and international influence. “African music is no longer simply a cultural phenomenon: it has become a force of influence. Our challenge now is to transform this influence into sustainable economic power. SIMA aims to build connections between creators, investors, institutions and markets so that the international visibility of our talents translates into measurable data, content monetization, economic opportunities, jobs and value creation for the continent.” Mamby Diomandé , Co-Founder of SIMA Three Priorities for Turning Creativity into Economic Power To address the challenges of a rapidly evolving global market, SIMA 2026 will structure its programme around three key priorities. The first focuses on competitiveness and internationalization, with the aim of strengthening the economic performance of industry stakeholders and facilitating the international export of African talent. The second emphasizes cross-sector collaboration, bringing music closer to fashion, film, tourism, sports and other creative industries in order to unlock new revenue opportunities. The third focuses on public policy, intellectual property and regulatory frameworks, with the ambition of developing concrete recommendations and strengthening the mechanisms that will enable the sector to better capture the value it generates. Beyond discussions and professional exchanges, SIMA aims to make creativity a genuine driver of connection across the ecosystem. Through its artist residency, live sessions and immersive formats, the event encourages collaboration between artists, producers, industry professionals and international stakeholders, while creating bridges between African markets and the international creative economy. A Week at the Crossroads of Creativity, Business and Influence From November 7–11, 2026, SIMA Lab. Music will bring together artists and beatmakers from across the continent for an artistic residency designed to produce a collaborative EP, with distribution by an international major label under consideration. On November 12–13, 2026, the professional days and panels will bring together key players from the music ecosystem to explore major issues shaping the future of the industry, including artificial intelligence, copyright, mobility, financing and emerging market opportunities. At the intersection of the cultural and sports industries, a dedicated session will also explore the convergence between football and music, two powerful drivers of influence across the continent, with the participation of sports executives and opinion leaders. As part of this dynamic, Makaya, SIMA’s showcase platform dedicated to discovering new talent, will spotlight emerging artists from Togo, Kenya, Madagascar and other African countries, providing a new stage for the next generation of talent. The programme will also feature the presentation of the Hamed Bakayoko Award, an honorary distinction recognizing the commitment of a patron to the development of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. On November 14, 2026, SIMA will extend the experience through a tourism circuit organized in collaboration with Benin Tourism, inviting artists, professionals and international guests to discover the heritage and iconic sites of Benin. This immersive experience will give participants an opportunity to gain a deeper understanding of the host country’s cultural, historical and tourism assets, while extending networking and exchanges beyond the professional framework of the event. About SIMA Created and initiated by music industry experts, the Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) promotes the African music industry, provides training and capacity-building opportunities for ecosystem stakeholders, and facilitates business connections between African and international industry players. As a true platform for connecting the cultural and creative industries, SIMA provides ecosystem stakeholders with a space to create, learn, share, connect and foster new collaborations, while contributing to discussions on the cultural, economic and technological issues shaping Africa’s creative industries and their international reach. item.title: Taiwan’s chipmaking giant TSMC to invest $1B in Anthropic, OpenAI
item.description: Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout. The chipmaker’s board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters . Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade shows signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported. But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal. Read full article Comments

item.title: Trump admin loses fight to spy on random journalists’ LinkedIn DMs
item.description: The Trump administration’s fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can’t sweep in “a vast number of confidential sources” of random journalists “who have no conceivable relationship” to the Department of Justice’s investigation, an appeals court ruled Tuesday. The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted. The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled. Read full article Comments

item.title: Ayra Starr Joins Coachella 2027 Lineup Alongside SZA, Dua Lipa & More
item.description: Ayra Starr returns with her third studio album, Starrgirl. Ayra Starr is taking her global run to another big stage! The Nigerian singer has been named among the performers at Coachella 2027, adding another major festival appearance to her growing list of international milestones. The Beninese-born singer, who rose to prominence as one of Afrobeats’ leading voices after joining Mavin Records, is set to perform on both weekends of the festival, Sunday, April 11, and Sunday, April 18, 2027. Coachella will take place at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. It’s been a big year for Ayra, with her third studio album, Starrgirl, adding to an already exciting run. Fans heading to the festival can look forward to hearing songs from the project, including “ Tornado ” and “ Midnight in New York “, as well as her collaboration “ Gimme Dat “. There’s also room for crowd favourites such as “ Rush “, “ Commas ” and “ Heaven Baby “. Ayra shares the Sunday bill with headliner SZA , alongside Victoria Monét , Jorja Smith , Becky G and Don Toliver . The wider festival, running from April 9 to 11 and April 16 to 18, will also feature headliners Dua Lipa and Tame Impala , with Madonna set for a special appearance in the dance tent. Her Coachella booking follows another major moment in London, where she performed at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as part of the NFL International Games halftime show, becoming the first African artist to headline the show. And there’s even more for fans to look forward to. Ayra has announced her 20-city Starrgirl World Tour , which will take her across Europe and North America in early 2027 before she heads to the California desert for Coachella. What a year ahead for the Starr girl. The official Coachella 2027 lineup featuring Nigerian singer Ayra Starr alongside headliners Dua Lipa, Tame Impala, and SZA at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. The Nigerian singer has been named among the performers at Coachella 2027, adding another major festival appearance to her growing list of international milestones. The Beninese-born singer, who rose to prominence as one of Afrobeats’ leading voices after joining Mavin Records, is set to perform on both weekends of the festival, Sunday, April 11, and Sunday, April 18, 2027. Coachella will take place at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. It’s been a big year for Ayra, with her third studio album, Starrgirl, adding to an already exciting run. Fans heading to the festival can look forward to hearing songs from the project, including “ Tornado ” and “ Midnight in New York “, as well as her collaboration “ Gimme Dat “. There’s also room for crowd favourites such as “ Rush “, “ Commas ” and “ Heaven Baby “. Ayra shares the Sunday bill with headliner SZA , alongside Victoria Monét , Jorja Smith , Becky G and Don Toliver . The wider festival, running from April 9 to 11 and April 16 to 18, will also feature headliners Dua Lipa and Tame Impala , with Madonna set for a special appearance in the dance tent. Her Coachella booking follows another major moment in London, where she performed at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as part of the NFL International Games halftime show, becoming the first African artist to headline the show. And there’s even more for fans to look forward to. Ayra has announced her 20-city Starrgirl World Tour , which will take her across Europe and North America in early 2027 before she heads to the California desert for Coachella. What a year ahead for the Starr girl. The official Coachella 2027 lineup featuring Nigerian singer Ayra Starr alongside headliners Dua Lipa, Tame Impala, and SZA at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. item.title: US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity
item.description: Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources. Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster , as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030. This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters. Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies. For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue. "Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam. "As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need." Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®

item.title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
item.description: The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game. This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity." Noting "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools," the group of jurors called out AI's ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still "not a foregone conclusion in our industry." Read full article Comments

item.title: Apple is shuttering its 28-year-old online community forum
item.description: Apple’s online community forum will close on November 20. On Tuesday night, Apple posted a message to the Apple Support Community announcing the forum's closure: The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site . We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products. For 28 years, the forum has provided Apple users with a way to get quick technical advice about their products. That advice usually came from fellow users, though Apple employees occasionally chimed in. As with any community forum, the helpfulness and accuracy of the advice varied. Read full article Comments

item.title: Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image
item.description: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error. To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today . In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said. He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image. "Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said. Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

item.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
item.description: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry. item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry. "It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke." Maybe life on Earth is a fluke It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet. However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth. Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA. However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars , because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity. "This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet." The 7 planets circling the star TRAPPIST-1, 3 of which might be able to keep liquid water on its surface. (Image credit: R. Hurt/T. Pyle/NASA) More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1 , where all the planets are bunched up close. In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive. The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports .

item.title: Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit
item.description: A swathe of Canonical's web services has been offline for hours, an awkward warm-up for tomorrow's Ubuntu Summit. Canonical's status page lists widespread disruption beginning at approximately 1100 UTC, affecting gopkg.in, Ubuntu cloud images and mailing lists, jaas.ai, the Ubuntu keyserver, Launchpad PPAs, the Livepatch API, canonical.com, Ubuntu login, maas.io, and 16 other services. Landscape is also affected. Email and the company's Discourse forums remain available. The Register has asked Canonical for more information but had received no response at publication time. The company suffered a DDoS attack last month , although the cause of this outage has not been confirmed. The timing is unfortunate. As the banner across the top of the Discourse forum page says: "The Ubuntu Summit starts tomorrow – join from anywhere!" The online event runs on November 12-13. For the first time since the 2022 Summit in Prague, The Reg FOSS desk won't be attending in person. Canonical is still experimenting with the format of the event, and the last few have been primarily online, with just a small in-person audience in its London offices. This is the second of two Summits this year, labeled 26.04 and 26.10 to mirror Ubuntu's release cycle. The timetable , hosted on the Discourse site, lists several talks on AI and agentic coding. The AI-heavy program we reported from June's event appears to be continuing. ®

item.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
item.description: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket . For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket . For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO. The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful. But SpaceX is phasing out the Falcon 9 — and its heavy-lift cousin, the Falcon Heavy — nonetheless, shifting all launch work over to its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which can haul more than 100 tons to LEO. There's a real worry among folks in the space community that this massive payload capacity won't be available to them for a while. SpaceX has made it pretty clear that early Starship operations will be geared toward internal priorities — specifically, the buildout of SpaceX's Starlink V3 broadband network and its Starmind AI data-center constellation. These will be very big jobs, even for the most powerful rocket ever built. For example, the Starlink V3 megaconstellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites , according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk . Starship can carry about 60 of these spacecraft to LEO per launch, so just building out the constellation will require about 1,700 liftoffs. The numbers for Starmind will be even more mind-boggling, for SpaceX wants that constellation to eventually harbor a million satellites . The coming launch bottleneck should increase demand for Electron as well as Neutron, Beck said during Monday's call. After all, many small-satellite operators have launched with SpaceX over the years, booking spots on Falcon 9 "rideshare" flights . And those opportunities are now drying up. "The next logical alternative is of course an Electron, so we see tremendous traction there," Beck said.

item.title: Omotunde’s 5 Days in South Korea: Exploring LG’s World of Innovation & Discovering the Best of Korean Culture

From exploring futuristic smart homes and AI-powered manufacturing facilities to tasting Korean street food, discovering Seoul, and experiencing the country’s rich culture, my 5-day South Korea adventure with LG Electronics was unforgettable. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Some trips leave you with beautiful photographs, others with unforgettable memories, and some leave you with a whole new perspective. My experience in South Korea with LG Electronics was a combination of all three. South Korea had been on my travel wish list for a while, so finally getting the opportunity to visit was exciting in itself. But this was more than just a trip to a new destination. It was an opportunity to explore the world of LG Electronics, understand its journey, experience its innovations firsthand and discover how technology continues to shape the way we live. Over five days, we explored different locations, met incredible people, exchanged ideas, experienced some of Korea’s most exciting innovations and, of course, made time to enjoy the country’s food, culture and lifestyle. From Seoul to Changwon , every day brought something new. Here’s a look at how the experience unfolded. While many of us know LG for its home appliances, televisions, and consumer electronics, the tour offered a much broader understanding of the brand and the thinking behind its innovations. At the LG Twin Towers, we were introduced to different aspects of the company’s business and got to explore some of its products and technologies, including the LG WashTower, InstaView refrigerator, Heat Pump Washer Dryer Combo, SolarDOM, and SKS premium appliances. Changwon Smart Park: Where AI, Robotics and Manufacturing Meet One of the most insightful experiences of the tour was visiting LG Smart Park in Changwon. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Before this visit, my idea of a manufacturing facility was largely shaped by traditional production lines and machinery. However, what I encountered at Changwon offered a completely different perspective. From the Heritage Lounge , where we got an introduction to LG’s manufacturing journey, to the Lighthouse Factory experience, there was so much to learn about how the company is integrating artificial intelligence, robotics, data and automation into its manufacturing processes. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Recognised by the World Economic Forum as a Lighthouse Factory, LG Smart Park demonstrates how advanced technologies can transform manufacturing and improve efficiency. Seeing how robots, intelligent systems and people work together was particularly fascinating. It also got me thinking about the ongoing conversations around artificial intelligence and the future of work. Rather than simply viewing AI as a technology that replaces human effort, I got to see how it can support people, take on repetitive tasks and improve the way complex processes are managed. It was one of those visits that makes you appreciate just how much goes on behind the products we use every day. LG Science Park: A Glimpse Into the Future Our next stop was LG Science Park in Magok, Seoul, one of the company’s major research and development hubs. This was another opportunity to see how LG is thinking about the future of technology and everyday living. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) We explored the LG AI Home experience, ThinQ Real Home, the Innovation Showroom and the D5 flagship experience. The demonstrations offered a glimpse into what connected living could look like, with smart technologies and appliances working together to create a more seamless home experience. Imagine a home where your appliances communicate with one another, respond intelligently to your needs and make everyday routines easier. That was the kind of future these experiences brought to life. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) It was fascinating seeing how research, technology and innovation are being translated into solutions that could eventually become part of our everyday lives. And just when I thought there was already so much to take in, I got to meet CLOiD ! View this post on Instagram A post shared by BellaNaija (@bellanaija) Meeting CLOiD: When the Future Becomes Real Meeting a live robot called CLOiD was definitely one of those surreal moments of the trip. We have seen robots in movies and watched countless videos of artificial intelligence and robotics, but seeing one up close and experiencing it in person is something else entirely. It was fascinating to see how far robotics has come and how these technologies are moving beyond futuristic concepts into real-world applications. Experiences like this make you pause and think about how different our everyday lives could look in the years ahead. The company’s story dates back to 1947, when it began as Lak Hui Chemical. In 1958, Goldstar was established, marking its entry into the electronics industry. The company eventually adopted the LG identity in 1995. Getting to see this journey represented through its history, milestones and innovations gave me a deeper appreciation of how the brand has evolved over the decades. It was particularly interesting learning about some of LG’s early milestones, including its first electric fan in 1960, refrigerator in 1965, air conditioner in 1968 and washing machine in 1969. From those early innovations to the smart appliances and technologies we explored during the tour, it was a remarkable reminder of how far the company has come. It also reinforced something I took away from the experience: innovation is not a one-time achievement. It requires continuous learning, improvement and the willingness to imagine what is possible beyond the present. Having spent the preceding days learning about LG’s history, exploring its manufacturing facilities and experiencing its smart home technologies, visiting the flagship store offered another opportunity to interact with the brand’s innovations in one space. The colours, visuals and immersive displays created such a beautiful cinematic experience. It was almost otherworldly, and I found myself completely immersed in the moment. Beyond the visual experience, it made me appreciate how far technology has come and the possibilities that innovation continues to create. item.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
item.description: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time. Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go. The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal. Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration. The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for. Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places. That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory. Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds. For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit , but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro. The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal. Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones. The reason, we're t

The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®

item.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
item.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

item.title: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
item.description: null The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange. But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed. M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini) What is it? The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus. M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity . Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old! Why is it amazing Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell. Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history. Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

item.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
item.description: Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch. Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products . However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services. The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling , with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update. At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. ® Updated to add on November 12: Microsoft has confirmed that there was indeed a problem with installing the update for some users, but the good news is that a fix is rolling out and no action is required on the part of customers (at least those connected to the internet and using Windows Update). The bad news is, alas, there appear to be a few issues with the update around printing and activation. Microsoft giveth, and Microsoft taketh away.

Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services. The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling , with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update. At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. ® Updated to add on November 12: Microsoft has confirmed that there was indeed a problem with installing the update for some users, but the good news is that a fix is rolling out and no action is required on the part of customers (at least those connected to the internet and using Windows Update). The bad news is, alas, there appear to be a few issues with the update around printing and activation. Microsoft giveth, and Microsoft taketh away.

item.title: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
item.description: Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky. The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set. "Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18. For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website. According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present. Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured. NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot." Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune. It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

item.title: Manchester United reach framework deal with Pochettino before settling Carrick’s fate
item.description: Pochettino wants to leave USA role for United United board meeting scheduled for Wednesday Manchester United have a framework agreement with Mauricio ­Pochettino for him to become their head coach if Michael Carrick is sacked. ­Carrick is expected to be fired in line with the recommendation from Jason ­Wilcox, the director of football, and Omar ­Berrada, the chief executive, to Sir Jim Ratcliffe. Pochettino is the USA men’s national team head coach and in August signed a contract to 2030 but he wants the United job after ­managing in the Premier League with Southampton, Tottenham and ­Chelsea. item.title: 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials
item.description: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses. Millions more HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users. The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match. Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB. NLB also claimed responsibility for an attack on Sberbank's internal systems at the same time, and later took partial credit for an attack on Alfa-Bank , Russia's largest private bank. ®
